paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: The Yellowstone hotspot is a volcanic hotspot located in the United States. It is responsible for volcanism on a large scale across Idaho, Montana, Nevada, Oregon and Wyoming. Today the hotspot lies under the Yellowstone Caldera. It is one of a few volcanic hotspots beneath the North American tectonic plate, and the Anahim hotspot is another.

paragraphs.heading: The Snake River Plain
paragraphs.text: A succession of caldera-forming eruptions from the hotspot made the eastern Snake River Plain. The calderas that resulted include Island Park, Henry's Fork and Bruneau-Jarbidge. The plain is a depression in the topography that cuts across Basin and Range mountain structures and runs more or less parallel to the motion of the North American Plate. Under its more recent basalts lie rhyolite lavas and ignimbrites, erupted while the lithosphere was passing over the hotspot. Younger volcanoes later covered the plain in places with young basalt lava flows, including at Craters of the Moon National Monument and Preserve.

paragraphs.heading: Early calderas in Nevada
paragraphs.text: On the Nevada–Oregon border lies the McDermitt volcanic field, which is often shown as the place where the hotspot first arrived. New dating and mapping show that this mid-Miocene volcanism affected a considerably larger area than was once appreciated. In northwest Nevada, three silicic calderas have been newly identified. Together with the Virgin Valley and McDermitt calderas, they are thought to have formed within a short interval, between 16.5 and 15.5 million years ago. The northwest Nevada calderas are 15 to 26 km across and laid down high-temperature rhyolite ignimbrites over roughly 5000 km².

paragraphs.heading: Ash that reached Nebraska
paragraphs.text: Between ten and twelve million years ago the Bruneau-Jarbidge volcanic field erupted. It spread a thick blanket of ash and formed a wide caldera. Within a hundred miles, animals were suffocated and burned in pyroclastic flows. Much farther away they died of slow suffocation and starvation. At Ashfall Fossil Beds in northeastern Nebraska, 1000 miles downwind, a foot of ash was laid down. Two hundred fossilized rhinoceros, along with many other animals, were preserved there in volcanic ash.

paragraphs.heading: The Heise eruptions
paragraphs.text: In eastern Idaho, the Heise volcanic field produced explosive eruptions that formed calderas. They began 6.6 million years ago and went on for more than 2 million years, with four large-volume rhyolitic eruptions one after another. The first three, the Blacktail, Walcott and Conant Creek tuffs, came to at least 2250 km³ of erupted magma. The last, the Kilgore Tuff, erupted 1800 km³ of ash 4.5 million years ago.

paragraphs.heading: The Yellowstone Plateau calderas
paragraphs.text: The Yellowstone Plateau volcanic field is made up of four adjacent calderas. The Island Park Caldera is older than the Henry's Fork Caldera and much larger, measuring roughly 58 miles (93 km) by 40 miles (64 km). The Henry's Fork Caldera sits nested inside it and was formed 1.3 million years ago in an eruption of more than 280 km³. The Yellowstone Caldera is the youngest of the hotspot's calderas. It formed 640,000 years ago and measures about 55 km by 72 km (34 by 45 miles). Of the many calderas the hotspot has formed, Henry's Fork is the only one that can be clearly seen at present.

paragraphs.heading: Since the last supereruption
paragraphs.text: Since the last supereruption, lava has erupted without explosions in and near the Yellowstone Caldera, and there have been explosive eruptions that were less violent. The most recent lava flow was about 70,000 years ago. The largest violent eruption dug out the West Thumb of Lake Yellowstone. That was around 150,000 years ago. Smaller steam explosions happen as well. One of them, 13,800 years ago, left a crater 5 kilometers across at Mary Bay on the edge of Yellowstone Lake.
